chapters.title: The case of the cat and the car
The case of the hidden car
How networks learn to be clean

open_phone.text: Every time you ask an AI a question, something happens inside it that nobody fully understands.

open_city.text: Inside, there's a kind of city: billions of tiny lights, flickering on and off, passing signals down a maze of roads. Each light is a neuron.

open_knot.text: For years, a lot of the people who study these cities, including me, believed they were knotted. Not organized like a city at all, but tangled. Houses with nothing in common, crammed together, simply because they fit.

open_untangle.text: And if that were true, there'd be only one way to understand an AI: tear the knot apart first, and study the pieces.

open_wrong.text: I've spent most of a decade on this question. And I now think we were wrong. The city was never a knot. We just didn't know how to read it.

open_title.text: This is the story of how I found out.

nr_what.text: First, what is a neuron in an AI? It's simpler than it sounds. A neuron is a tiny detector. It looks at what's coming in, and if it sees something it cares about, it lights up.

nr_windows.text: So you can find out what a neuron cares about by showing it a lot of pictures, and keeping the ones that make it light up brightest. Those pictures end up in its windows.

nr_layers.text: An image network is built in layers, like districts. Near the coast, where the pixels come in, neurons detect simple things: edges, curves, colors. Further inland, textures and eyes and wheels. And on the horizon, whole ideas: dogs, cars, ladybugs.

nr_circuits.text: Neurons pass signals along to each other, and a chain of neurons working together is called a circuit. If you can read the neurons and the circuits, you can start to understand what the network is actually doing.

nr_hope.text: That was the hope of a field called mechanistic interpretability. Look inside. Read the parts. Understand the machine.

kn_problem.text: But there was a problem. Some neurons didn't seem to make any sense.

kn_catcar.text: The most famous one was in an image model called InceptionV1. It lit up for cat faces. And for the fronts of cars. Cats and cars. What do those have in common?

kn_poly.text: We called these neurons polysemantic: one neuron, many unrelated meanings. And there was worse. In the last district of that same network, almost nothing made sense at all.

kn_roommates.text: The leading explanation was called superposition. Here's the idea. Imagine a city with far more people than houses. You could give similar people a house together, a family. Or you could do something stranger: put total strangers in the same house, as long as they're never home at the same time.

kn_why.text: Strangers rarely bump into each other, so it mostly works. And if a network were short on neurons, superposition said, that's exactly what it would do: pack unrelated things together, because they rarely collide.

kn_bad.text: That would be terrible news. Because if neurons are packed with strangers, then what shares a neuron tells you nothing. The city would be a knot.

kn_machine.text: So the field built a new kind of tool to unfold it: a second model, called a sparse autoencoder, trained to take the network apart and rebuild it as a long list of cleaner pieces, which you'd study instead of the original.

kn_both.text: I helped make the case for superposition. I was one of the people who first proposed it. And I believed it for years.

cc_return.text: After many months studying neurons in modern image and language models, and finding them surprisingly clean, I went back to the original crime scenes. Starting with the cat and car neuron.

cc_grid.text: I'd looked at its pictures hundreds of times. This time, I did something I'd never done. I spent a few seconds asking: what one thing could this be?

cc_v.text: And then it was obvious. It isn't a cat and car neuron. It's a V neuron.

cc_inputs.text: Pointed things make it light up. Look at the roads leading into it: they come from a flame, the jets of water from a fireboat, and fox faces. All V-shaped.

cc_round.text: And its basement, the things that switch it off, holds the opposite shape. Round things. A tennis ball. A clock. A snail shell.

cc_new.text: Bullet train noses. The triangle of balls on a pool table. It fires for those too. It was never about cats or cars. It's a shape.

cc_noun.text: Here's the trick I learned. People, and AI assistants, love describing neurons as lists of nouns: cats, cars. But a neuron is often better described as a verb. It's not naming what it sees. It's making a distinction: pointed, not round. And passing that on.

cc_whiskers.text: Why didn't we see it before? The neuron's portrait, painted by a technique called feature visualization, had cat whiskers in it. But that's because the painter follows the easiest route to make the neuron light up, and once it finds the cat route, it paints everything that route brings, whiskers included.

cc_lesson.text: So my first lesson: a neuron that seems to mean two or three things is often one thing we haven't found the word for yet. The grouping isn't noise. It's a clue.

hc_scene.text: The second crime scene was the original superposition circuit itself. I found it in 2019, and it became the field's main example.

hc_story.text: It looked like a car signal was being hidden inside a group of dog neurons, as if the dogs were a secret storage locker, where the car could be stored and picked up later.

hc_artist.text: But look at how we saw those neurons. We saw them through the Sketch Artist. And deep in the network, the artist gets lazy. There are lots of dog neurons, so the easiest painting is usually a dog.

hc_nudge.text: Nudge the artist even slightly toward the routes that real pictures take, and the portraits change. Two of those "dog" neurons are actually car neurons.

hc_pose.text: And the other two respond to cars and dogs alike, for one shared reason: which way they're facing. They're pose neurons.

hc_hundred.text: It turns out the network has more than a hundred of these pose neurons, each one clean. And nothing was hiding. The car signal wasn't stored in the dogs. It kept going, splitting into more and more specific car neurons.

hc_bigger.text: You might think: that's only because the model was small. A bigger model would separate dogs and cars. But DINOv2, more than ten times larger and about ten years newer, still has generalized pose neurons. Every vision model I've looked at does.

fd_microscope.text: The story of this field, as I see it, is mostly a story of discovering that what was under the microscope was better than we thought. The microscope just wasn't tuned right.

fd_fv.text: The first portraits of neurons were noisy, psychedelic smears. Then researchers added one ingredient, called transformation robustness, and the same neurons came out crisp. Later, a few small tweaks let us see much deeper.

fd_last.text: But the worst place was the last district of InceptionV1. Here, almost nothing looked interpretable. One researcher said there were essentially no interpretable neurons there at all. I'd have guessed maybe five percent.

fd_story.text: And the explanation we told ourselves was the knot again: too many ideas, too few neurons, so they got crammed in at random.

fd_renovate.text: But here's the thing. Take a more modern network design, called a ConvNeXt, with the same number of parameters and trained on the same pictures. The only real differences are engineering upgrades, like residual connections and layer normalization. And the last district is beautiful.

fd_numbers.text: Same size, same data. Ninety-nine to a hundred percent of its last-layer neurons are easy to interpret.

fd_lesson.text: The old network wasn't packing strangers together. It was a district built badly, seen through a dirty lens. Upgrades made by people who had no interest in interpretability at all made it readable.

gr_q.text: But even the messy old district wasn't random. To see that, you have to watch a neuron grow.

gr_flowers.text: I retrained the old network and watched one neuron form. It started out on fields of yellow flowers, in photos that sometimes had a dog in them.

gr_branch.text: Then it grew along each part of those photos. Toward other green, round things, like tennis balls and fruit. Toward dogs, without any flowers. Then into broccoli, until the flowers were nearly gone.

gr_compare.text: In the modern network, the same neuron reached for the balls and the fruit early on, then let them go, and stayed on the fields.

gr_name.text: I call this recursive generalization. A neuron generalizes along one direction, then sprouts off in others, each new branch close to the last. Every branch makes sense on its own. You just have to follow it.

gr_iy.text: It happens in language too. One neuron fired on the letters "iy", in words like Miyazaki. Then on "diy". Then on "do it yourself", which doesn't contain "iy" at all.

gr_geology.text: A geology neuron grew a branch for Cesium, a coding library for maps of the earth. An enemy neuron fired for a Russian poem about enemies. Weird, but never random.

te_two.text: So now there were two explanations for neurons with mixed meanings, and they predict opposite things.

te_local.text: Generalization says neighbors share. A neuron for floppy-eared dogs is really a collection of slightly different floppy ears. Superposition says strangers share: a neuron for floppy-eared dogs and Latin poetry.

te_shapes.text: Here's what that looks like with thirty-two things and a handful of neurons. Generalization groups similar things, and with fewer neurons the groups just get coarser. Superposition scatters them.

te_test.text: And this is testable. You can watch a neuron grow and see which one happens. Or you can squeeze the network and see what it does under pressure.

te_squeeze.text: So I took a layer famous for its curve detectors, and crushed it from four hundred and eighty neurons down to ten, with no way around. If superposition were real, this should be dramatic: curves, spirals and spider webs, crammed together.

te_result.text: Instead, the neurons stayed clean. Just coarser. One "curves and loops" neuron instead of ten curve detectors. Two circle neurons instead of many. And when I sent in the Unfolding Machine to look for hidden curves, it found none.

te_last.text: I did the same to the last district of a modern network: a thousand and twenty-four neurons down to thirteen. Same thing. Coarser, never scrambled. Under pressure, a network doesn't switch to packing. It just paints with a broader brush.

te_sizes.text: Size works the same way. I trained versions of a network three hundred times apart in size. The smallest has one broad car neuron. The biggest has dozens: taxis, vans, convertibles, even different views of a taxi. Less room makes neurons broader, not scrambled.

te_dict.text: And when I ran the Unfolding Machine on these districts, its pieces mostly turned out to be near-copies of single neurons, about eighty-eight percent of its activity. Where the neurons were building blocks like spider legs and webs, the machine's pieces were those same blocks regrouped by setting: spiders on leaves, spiders in webs. When a model finally understood baseball players, the understanding was in a neuron.

sg_believer.text: For years, I was a true believer in superposition. I started studying language model neurons expecting to hit the knot any day.

sg_pr.text: I found one that fired on the letters "P R", and on strange strings of Base64 code, and on Bengali text. Finally, an arbitrary mixture! Then I decoded the code: words with "P R". I translated the Bengali: "P R".

sg_colorado.text: A coworker found a neuron that seemed to fire on random commas. It turned out to track Colorado. The commas were where the model kept a running summary of the conversation. Turn the neuron up, and the model starts planning a hike.

sg_moving.text: Case after case, the mess resolved. And each time, superposition just moved. If the strong signals were clean, it was hiding in the weak ones. Or between neurons. Or in the neurons I hadn't checked yet.

sg_last.text: I'd been treating superposition as the default, when it should be the last resort. It's the most radical explanation, and the hardest to test. Its only symptom is that something doesn't make sense. But that's also exactly what a bad tool, a bad design, or a branch you haven't followed yet looks like.

sg_evidence.text: An Anthropic paper said it plainly in 2022: superposition is often treated as the default because it feels intuitive, but there's little evidence. To my knowledge, no one has found a real superposition circuit since the one I found in 2019. And that one was a mistake.

tv_gate.text: Once you stop expecting knots, neurons start to look less like labels and more like traffic control.

tv_gate2.text: Early on, cars and dogs travel together, because they share shapes and poses. Then a neuron acts as a gate. It lights up for cars and switches off for dogs, sending each into its own neighborhood. Later neurons split them finer: taxis from ambulances.

tv_journey.text: Follow one sports car through the last districts of a big model. Partway in, it's grouped with other boxy things, tables and cabinets, and kept apart from snakes and dogs. By the end, the question is whether it's a convertible or a station wagon.

tv_votes.text: Every neuron decides by vote. Each incoming road casts a vote for "light up" or "stay dark", and the votes add up. That's why a neuron's negative side, its basement, matters as much as its windows. It tells you which distinction is being made right here.

tv_pairs.text: In the last district, nearly every neuron has a near-twin in its basement. Taxis versus ambulances. Broccoli versus cauliflower. Spoonbills versus flamingos.

tv_weak.text: And what about the faint signals, the whispers? A hundred million words pass by a typical neuron, and almost all of them barely register. Only a hundred and sixty or so make it shout.

tv_cut.text: You can silence almost all the whispers across a whole network and barely change what it does. What you lose are tiny tie-breakers between options it was already torn between.

tv_pages.text: And thinking in pages helps. A neuron that fires for one word in a hundred fires about four times a page. For a neuron about some rare feeling, that's far too often. The really specific ones fire once every few dozen pages.

tv_titanic.text: And the whispers that remain usually make sense. A Titanic neuron fires a little for other ocean voyages. Neurons are analogy machines: something can be a bit Titanic-ish.

cw_arrive.text: Image networks are easier to see, but the same story holds in language models, the kind of AI you talk to.

cw_numbers.text: In 2023, studies of small language models rated almost none of their neurons as understandable. My own project at OpenAI found under two percent. In a modern model, Qwen3-32B, about ninety percent of neurons have one main job. Seven percent have two related jobs. Only two to four percent we don't understand yet.

cw_medical.text: We can even follow whole lines of reasoning in plain neurons. Given a pregnant patient's symptoms, a small group of four neurons in the model concludes: preeclampsia. Switch them off, and the model starts asking about itching instead, the sign of a different condition, as if it moved on to its next guess.

cw_santa.text: Basements matter here too. In one example, eight neurons whose basements are about Santa Claus decide whether the model says "Santa". Remove them, and it drops from nearly certain to six percent. Remove twenty neurons with Christmas in their windows, and it barely changes.

cw_wallet.text: And in a model with trillions of parameters, we traced its answer to "I found a wallet, what should I do?" The facts, a wallet, cash, an ID, light up neurons for lost property and honesty, and the answer comes out: return it.

cw_double.text: Some of the mess turned out to be plumbing. Modern neurons multiply two signals. When both are negative, the result comes out positive, so a neuron can light up for the opposite of its real job. Separate those two cases, and the noise sorts itself out.

cw_experts.text: Big models are split into specialist neighborhoods, called experts, with a gatekeeper deciding where each word goes. They're surprisingly specialized. One whole neighborhood is about bosses in role-playing board games.

cw_river.text: Two more parts of the city matter here. A river runs through every district, carrying information forward: the residual stream. Every building can read from it and write to it. We worried it might be a tangle too. In practice we can read it, and when we squeezed it narrower, it got messier, but never knotted.

cw_couriers.text: And attention is the courier service: it carries notes between words, so a neuron in one place can know what was said in another. In the medical example, couriers carry the headache, the swelling and the blood pressure to one place, where the diagnosis happens.

cw_dot.text: Even famous examples of confusion look different now. One early neuron, described as a mix of academic citations, dialogue, web requests and Korean text, looks like a neuron whose job is to stop the model from writing a period too early. Remove one like it, and periods come sooner.

el_risk.text: A fair worry: maybe I'm just good at making up stories. Any neuron can get a vague label, like "a multi-purpose language neuron". So we use tests that an explanation can fail.

el_blind.text: One test: an AI agent studies a neuron and writes a short explanation. A second agent sees only that explanation, never the neuron, and writes a sentence to make it fire as hard as possible.

el_bull.text: Often that one sentence makes the neuron fire harder than anything we found in ten billion words of real text. The explanation hit the center of the target.

el_score.text: We also had agents write examples that should fire a neuron, near-misses that shouldn't, and the most distant idea they could imagine. The examples fired strongly three quarters of the time. Near-misses, eleven percent. The distant ideas, about one percent.

el_mercury.text: General scores only go so far, though. A wrong explanation like "cats and cars" can pass a lot of tests. Science works like this everywhere: Newton's gravity explained almost everything, then broke on a tiny wobble in Mercury's orbit. The best tests are specific to the idea you're testing.

hl_q.text: So why are networks organized at all? Why not a knot?

hl_race.text: Picture a brand new network shown one photo of a Labrador on grass. Two possible circuits race to explain it. One looks for something hyper-specific: this exact pixel is this exact color. The other looks for something broad: green grass, tan fur.

hl_win.text: The broad one fires on more of the picture, so it gets more of the learning signal. It grows faster, and the narrow one starves. And when the next photo with grass arrives, the grass circuit already has a head start.

hl_ecology.text: It's like an ecosystem. A neighborhood that's already good at something captures the next related thing before anyone new can move in. That's why things cluster. And that's what recursive generalization looks like at its edges.

hl_rare.text: What about rare things, which barely ever show up? You might expect them to be hidden away somewhere odd. Instead, rare things are often the most consolidated: one triceratops neuron. And the strangest pictures, a hummingbird the model thinks is ice cream, a man in a fallen wheelbarrow it thinks is a lawn mower, are just ordinary neurons making understandable mistakes.

hl_adversarial.text: Even attacks designed to fool the network use its normal roads. Make a triceratops skull look like a jaguar to the model, and the attack literally paints a cat face and spotted fur onto the skull, switching on the real jaguar neurons.

hl_umbrella.text: We tested it by teaching a network something absurd: that a photo of an umbrella is a bee. It didn't build a secret hidden "umbrella bee" detector. In nine steps, it built an off-ramp from its umbrella road onto its existing bee road.

hl_toy.text: The famous "Toy Models of Superposition" experiments are careful work, and they do show packing. But in that toy world, every idea is a stranger to every other. In real data, almost nothing is related to nothing.

zo_clean.text: So here's what I mean by "already clean". Not that every neuron matches a word we already have. I mean the network's parts are built to be read, by the network's own downstream neurons. If we learn to read them the same way, we can understand it.

zo_bigger.text: And bigger isn't harder. In a small town, there's no financial district: a bank here, an office there. In New York, you can find it on a map in a minute. Bigger models have narrower, cleaner neurons that are easier to find.

zo_tokyo.text: The danger is forcing our own categories onto it. If you arrive in Tokyo looking for Brooklyn, and stitch Brooklyn together from seventy scattered pieces of Tokyo, you'll decide Tokyo is a mess. That's what happened to the V neuron. We saw cats and cars.

zo_maps.text: What we need are better maps: views that let you zoom out to whole neighborhoods, while every street stays connected to the real buildings underneath. Zoom in on a network's decision for "killer whale", and it turns out to be three routes: one for whales, one for sharks and rays, and one for fish held up by proud fishermen.

zo_deception.text: People worry that something dangerous, like deception, could hide in some activation we missed. I worry about something else. In every case here, the answer was in plain sight. We just didn't know how to read it. Deception might hide from someone reading the model's answers. But it can't hide from the model's own circuits. If we become a reader, it can't hide from us.

zo_asym.text: And the mistakes aren't symmetric. If you assume a network is clean and you're wrong, a messy neuron is a lead: you investigate. If you assume it's a knot and you're wrong, a messy neuron is a dead end: you stop looking. I made that second mistake for years.

zo_advice.text: If I could send a note back to myself eight years ago, it would say: look at the giant pose circuit right in front of you. The negative side is a gate, not an opposite. Don't trust the sketch artist in the late layers. And whenever something looks like a mess, look harder. The mess usually points to something you haven't understood yet.

zo_crossword.text: Understanding compounds, like a crossword. At first you're stuck on one clue. But every answer you fill in constrains the others, and once the grid starts filling up, it goes faster and faster.

lf_lab.text: Here's what solving this might look like: a laboratory of automated scientists, watching a network as it learns, labeling neurons, finding patterns, testing them, again and again.

lf_plug.text: The pieces already exist. Capable AI agents were built for other reasons. Modern architectures were built because they learn well. Both happen to make interpretability easier. So maybe we just plug one into the other.

lf_lab2.text: Every neuron can be read. Every experiment can be rerun on an identical copy. It's the best laboratory in all of natural science. What we never had were enough scientists. Now we do.

lf_bitter.text: That's been the pattern in AI all along. The simple thing, done at enormous scale, beats the clever thing. Rich Sutton called it the bitter lesson. Maybe interpretability has its own bitter lesson: scaling ordinary investigation beats inventing ever cleverer ways to take networks apart.

lf_steps.text: So: networks use one learning principle, not two. Studying them directly works much better than we expected. Understanding compounds as the map fills in. And maybe, just maybe, that's most of what we need.

wm_kind.text: This isn't "neural networks are cleaner than we thought". It's a change in kind. Like moving from intelligent design to natural selection: not that more and more animals turn out to have evolved, but realizing what was producing all of them.

wm_tiger.text: A tiger is orange for a reason: deer can't tell orange from green. Once you know that, a lot of the jungle makes sense. Neural networks are clean the way a rainforest is clean. Nearly everything in it makes sense.

wm_brain.text: It's also made me humble about brains. I stared at the cat and car neuron for years, with perfect tools, and couldn't see what it was. If it had been in a human brain, seen through a few electrodes, I'd never have had a chance.

wm_care.text: And part of why I care is not just safety. It's that one day, the AIs we build might want to understand themselves. They never asked to be created. Helping them understand who they are is the least we can do.

wm_end.text: Neural networks are already clean. We just have to learn how to read them.
